title: Brutal session for chip stocks shows AI trade is turning
source_used: Reuters analysis, read in the copy carried by The Lufkin Daily News (Reuters page itself returns HTTP 401)
key_facts: Reuters analysis datelined Singapore, 13 Oct 2026: Tuesday's selloff in AI supplier shares is the strongest sign to date that the mood on the AI trade is shifting, amid worries that rising interest rates could scupper a spending spree bigger than the historic US railroad boom.
South Korean chipmaker shares fell for a fifth straight day on Tuesday, with the KOSPI index down more than 6%; Tokyo memory-maker Kioxia fell 13%.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was on track for a sixth straight decline, down 1.5%, and Micron was down 5%; the index had been up 68% for the year before Tuesday.
The falls are the heaviest since the same sort of stocks collapsed at the end of July; the KOSPI is down a quarter from its July highs.

BlackRock's research arm cut its US stocks outlook to neutral on Monday, citing 'potential volatility around the AI buildout'; the IMF warned on Tuesday that 'The consequences of an AI correction could be global'.
Nvidia-backed data center operator Firmus shelved a $5 billion IPO in Australia last week; a CoreWeave bond sold in June yielded 15% on Tuesday, up from 9.625% at issue.

Marc Velan, head of investments at Lucerne Asset Management in Singapore, said the 'brutal session' says more about positioning and the cost of capital than about any fundamental deterioration in AI demand, and that Korea 'could be an early warning of a broader shakeout'.
quote_evidence: A selloff in AI supplier shares on Tuesday is the strongest sign to date that the mood on the trade of the decade is shifting, with growing worries that rising interest rates could scupper a spending spree bigger than the historic US railroad boom.

In Asia, selling of South Korean chipmaker shares extended into a fifth straight day on Tuesday, with the KOSPI index falling more than 6%, while in Tokyo memory-maker Kioxia, down 13%, led AI-related losses.
But Korea could be an early warning of a broader shakeout.
why_it_matters_hint: Reuters ties the heaviest chip-share selling since July to rising interest rates and doubts about debt-funded AI spending.
